The reproductive biology of the Giant Hummingbird (Patagona gigas) begins with the incubating bird egg, a stage during which development proceeds within a calcareous shell. The incubation period, which is the interval from egg laying to the emergence of the altricial nestling, lasts between 12 and 13 days, with a mean recorded age at hatching of 12.5 days [ab = 12.5 days] when eggs are maintained at a stable incubation temperature of 32 °C [T = 32 °C]. Newly hatched chicks are entirely dependent on parental provisioning and possess a remarkably small initial wet body mass of only 1.78 grams [Ww0 = 1.78 grams]. This minimal mass at emergence reflects the high energetic cost of producing a clutch within the constraints of a hovering foraging mode. Field observations indicate that females typically lay two eggs per clutch [N_R_i = two eggs per clutch], with a single clutch produced each year [F_R_i = single clutch produced each year], a modest reproductive rate consistent with the life-history strategy of a large-bodied, long-lived bird in a climatically unpredictable high-altitude environment.

During the subsequent nestling phase, the developing chick undergoes a period of rapid growth and feather development before achieving flight capability. Under the thermal conditions characteristic of active metabolic periods in this species, measured at a body temperature of 38.1 °C [T = 38.1 °C], fledging occurs approximately 20 days after hatching [tx = approximately 20 days after hatching]. By this developmental milestone, the young bird reaches a wet weight at fledging of 16 grams [Wwx = 16 grams], representing a substantial increase over its initial hatching mass. The duration of the nestling period is relatively brief for a bird of this ultimate size, a pattern that may be linked to the necessity of reducing predation risk in exposed montane nesting sites. After leaving the nest, the fledgling continues to receive parental care for a short period, gradually transitioning to independent foraging on nectar and small arthropods. The post-fledging phase is critical, as the immature bird must hone its hovering skills, a metabolically demanding feeding technique that requires precise neuromuscular coordination and substantial wing muscle development before achieving adult-like proficiency.

As the juvenile bird matures, it undergoes significant somatic growth toward its ultimate adult dimensions. Field measurements indicate that sexually mature females attain a maximum adult body mass of 19.8 grams [Wwi = 19.8 grams], while their male counterparts reach a slightly larger adult mass of 22 grams [Wwi = 22 grams]. This modest sexual size dimorphism, with males being on average about 11 percent heavier than females, may reflect the selective pressures of male-male competition for access to high-quality feeding territories. The attainment of adult mass occurs gradually over the first several months of life, and the process involves a progressive replacement of juvenile plumage with iridescent adult feathers. Under the standard thermal conditions typical of the species' active metabolic state (38.1 °C [T = 38.1 °C]), puberty is reached at approximately 200 days after hatching [tp = approximately 200 days after hatching], marking the onset of gonadal maturation and the ability to engage in reproductive behavior. This timing is consistent with a single annual breeding season that coincides with the peak flowering period in the Andean highlands.

The first successful reproductive event in the life of a Giant Hummingbird is deferred relative to the attainment of sexual maturity. Under the metabolic regime maintained at 38.1 °C [T = 38.1 °C], the time since birth at the first brood is 365 days [tR = 365 days], meaning that most individuals do not breed until their second calendar year of life. This delay between reaching puberty and initiating reproduction may be an adaptive strategy, allowing young birds to accumulate sufficient fat reserves and establish a stable feeding territory capable of supporting the energetic demands of egg production and chick provisioning. The species' maximum reproductive rate, while low in terms of annual fecundity, is consistent with a life-history strategy that prioritizes adult survival in a challenging environment. Banding studies and recapture data from long-term monitoring programs in the Andes have provided valuable insight into the species' longevity, revealing that the maximum lifespan recorded for Patagona gigas under natural conditions is approximately 10.2 years [am = approximately 10.2 years] when measured at a body temperature of 38.1 °C [T = 38.1 °C].

In comparison to other hummingbird species, the Giant Hummingbird occupies an extreme position on several life-history axes, particularly in terms of its large body size and extended longevity. While smaller sympatric species such as the Andean Hillstar may experience higher annual mortality rates and shorter lifespans, Patagona gigas appears to exhibit a slower pace of life, with a maximum longevity of roughly 10.2 years [am = roughly 10.2 years] at a body temperature of 38.1 °C [T = 38.1 °C] setting it apart from most trochilids. The relatively low annual reproductive output, characterized by a single clutch raised per year [F_R_i = a single clutch raised per year], containing two eggs [N_R_i = containing two eggs], aligns with theoretical predictions for a species that invests heavily in self-maintenance and survival in a resource-limited montane ecosystem. The large adult body mass—19.8 grams [Wwi = 19.8 grams] in females and 22 grams [Wwi = 22 grams] in males—confers several physiological advantages, including a lower mass-specific metabolic rate and greater thermal inertia, which may reduce daily energetic costs during cold Andean nights. These traits collectively paint a portrait of a species that has evolved a conservative life-history strategy, trading high fecundity for exceptional longevity and the capacity to persist in one of the most demanding avian habitats on Earth.
